result:
Here is a free-write on whatever surfaces:

The old wooden desk in the corner of my grandmother's house had a knot in it shaped like a sleeping cat. I used to trace its outline with my fingertip during long Sunday afternoons when the adults were talking in low voices about things I wasn't supposed to hear. The desk was mine, sort of, though I never claimed ownership. It simply became the place where I went when the world felt too loud, which was often. Cats in wood, I learned later, are called burls, and they happen when a tree gets sick or injured and grows in strange, beautiful ways around the wound. I think about that a lot, how the most interesting parts of things are usually the parts that got hurt.

There's a particular quality to September light that makes me feel like I'm being gently called somewhere. Not urgently. Just a low, persistent hum of invitation. I walked to school through that kind of light for twelve years, and now I walk to a train, and the light follows me still, slightly different each time, but always that same September gold. My mother used to say the light slants in autumn because the earth is tired of standing straight. I believed her until I was embarrassingly old.

I've been thinking about the word "liminal" too much lately. It used to mean something specific to anthropologists, thresholds and passages and the space between. Now people use it to describe any mild feeling of in-betweenness, which is a shame because the real thing deserves its own word. I think I'm in a liminal space in my life, though I hate to say it like that, like I'm performing my own uncertainty for an audience. The truth is messier. The truth is I don't know what I'm doing and I suspect I never did, and the people who look like they know are mostly just better at improvising.

My dog is snoring on the couch right now. She does this thing where her paws twitch when she dreams, and I find it unbearably sweet, the idea that she has whole worlds happening behind those closed eyes, worlds I will never be invited into. I hope they're good worlds. I hope there's an endless field and someone throwing a ball and all the table scraps she wants. She has a tumor on her spleen, or maybe she doesn't. The vet wasn't sure. We're waiting. Waiting is its own kind of weather.

I used to believe that if I read enough books I would become wise, and now I have read many books and I am not wise, only familiar with the particular shape of my own ignorance. This is, I'm told, a kind of progress. The Greeks had a word for it too, probably. They had words for everything, which is one reason their civilization fell, some say, though I think that's reductive and also probably not true.

My favorite sound is rain on a window when I'm already inside and warm and have nowhere to be. My second favorite sound is the particular silence after everyone has gone home from a party, when the house exhales and you can hear the fridge humming and the clock doing its patient work. My third favorite sound is a child's voice calling from another room, "Mom?" — just that, just the word, just the small bell of needing.

I have a scar on my left knee from when I was seven. I fell off a fence chasing a neighbor's cat, a fat orange thing named Buster who didn't want to be caught and shouldn't have been. The scar is shaped like a comma, which I think is fitting, since my whole life feels like a comma sometimes, this pause in the middle of a sentence I can't see the end of yet.

I made my peace a long time ago with the fact that I will never be the person who fixes things. I am the person who sits with things. I am the person who makes tea and listens and says, "That sounds really hard," and means it. I used to think this made me useless. Now I think it might be the only thing I have to offer, which is a different thing entirely.

The bread I baked this morning is still warm. There's a small dent in the top where I forgot to slash it, and it came out lopsided and a little ugly and entirely edible. I'll have some with butter and salt for lunch. The butter is from a farm two towns over. The salt is from a jar that has been in my cupboard so long I've forgotten where it came from. This, I think, is a kind of wealth.

I should go. But first, the comma on my knee, the dog dreaming, the bread, the light. These are the things I wanted to remember.
